publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Vice-President): On page 27 of the Journal, Mr. Brunner refers to the desirability of a further standardisation in practical methods. It has often struck me that when considering a business such as the gold mining industry, an ideal case could be made out for standardisation. While differences in mining methods exist they are, I take it, relatively minor ones, general practice being more or less standard on these fields. If this is so, then it seems to me that a policy of standardisation would result in very considearble economies both in capital and operation charges. It is clear that if standard specifications of motors and switchgear and any other plant, whether electrical or mechanical, could be worked to by the manufacturers, the cost of production would be materially reduced. I suppose one might apply this argument to many articles in general use on the mines, and while opportunities for effecting economies may have been lost in the past, there may be still sufficient expansion ahead of us to make a closer standardisation worth while.

articleTitle: The fundamentals of radio, particularly in regard to reception
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: As it is the object of this paper to explain in some small degree the fundamental principle of radio, it would perhaps be better, at the commencement, to explain the difference between radio and audio frequency. Under normal conditions the highest audible note has a frequency in the vicinity of 15,000 to 16,000, and any frequency above that is generally considered radio frequency. The wave length is the distance (generally expressed in terms of metres) between any two peaks of the wave. These waves are sent out into the ether in a definite form and retain that form until completely exhausted; they do, however, lose in amplitude, and, therefore, although the wave does not lessen in length between the peaks, the height of the peaks dwindle by degrees until such time as the energy is completely exhausted.

I wondered if Mr. Bullock could explain how corrosion could be positively avoided on this gear when operating with coal containing, say, three per cent, of sulphur. There are such coals in South Africa. From the description of the gear, I gather that the narrow channels in the corrugated plates are scoured every hour or so with a jet of steam. It seems to me that, with coal of high sulphur content, you there have all the conditions necessary for not only corrosion, but actual dissolution of the metal from sulphurous acid, this repeated scouring of the surface of the metal presents continually a clean surface to the action of the sulphur itself, and the sulphur gases dissolved in the moisture give us sulphurous acid.

articleTitle: Economics of electric transmission and feeder systems for urban electrical supply
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: One of the most important subjects before the electric supply industry at the present time is that of distribution of current, and by distribution in this instance I mean the conveyance of current from the point or points of generation to the places at which it is to be utilised. The science of generation has been studied and improved tremendously during the last few years, in fact, steady progress has been made in Power Station machinery and methods ever since the commencement of the commercial production of electricity as regards both continuity of service as well as economy of production. Many engineers living to-day have been actively engaged in the industry from its earliest days, and have followed the progress made from the time when rough measurements were first made of the quantity of coal used to produce a kilowatt hour, being then from 5 lbs. to 10 lbs., till the present time, when we closely determine the British Thermal Units needed per unit and have already reached such a figure on an average not more than one-fifth of what prevailed 25 years ago. I say already, because further almost revolutionary improvements in the process of converting the potential heat in fuel to electricity are being tried out or proposed, and the next generation is likely to see present average figures cut in half at least, for these new methods include the pulverizing of fuel, the use of steam pressures of 1,200 lbs. per square inch, the employment of mercury vapour as the working fluid, and the very latest referred to by Mr. Otley in his recent address to the South African Intitution of Engineers, a complete reconsideration of the means of converting water into steam by substituting superheaters for the ordinary boilers. The result of some or all of these methods in combination gives us grounds for hope that in the not very distant future a kilowatt hour will be generated at an expenditure of not more than 10,000 or 12,000 B.T.U.s, and the significance of this outlook is that the commercial applications of electricity will be vastly extended and, in fact, light, heat and power will be exclusively obtained through the medium of the passage of an electric current, for if we can send out a kilowatt for an hour at the expenditure of no more than a pound of coal nothing else except water power will be able to compete as a prime mover, and even water power will be in the field only in those cases where it is fairly easy of development and where expensive dams and long pipe lines and transmission lines are not required. We may be in the way to see another swing of the pendulum, and those countries with plentiful deposits of cheap coal in reasonable proximity to condensing water may come into the picture again as cheap electricity producers for electro-chemical and steel making industries.
